meta.title: Focus Area 1 — Health in an Australian and Global Context
meta.range: Year 12 · Data-driven & source-based · one of the two focus areas examined in the HSC exam

boxes.label: Examinable
boxes.bodyHtml: How healthy Australians are, measured through epidemiology, morbidity, mortality and life expectancy; groups experiencing health inequities; Australia compared with OECD countries; chronic conditions (cardiovascular disease, cancer and one other); an ageing population; how the Australian healthcare system works, is funded and shares responsibility across government and non-government sectors; the role of technology, digital health and big data; and how the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs 3, 4, 10 and 11) can inform strategies to improve a community's health.

boxes.label: Format reminder
boxes.bodyHtml: The HSC exam draws on content from both Year 12 focus areas — this one and Training for Improved Performance — so revise them together rather than in isolation.

summary.note: Organised by the syllabus's four key questions for this focus area.

groups.title: CQ1 — How healthy are Australians?
points: Epidemiology is the branch of medical science that studies the causes, distribution and control of disease and injury across populations — it identifies broad health trends but doesn't fully explain the sociocultural factors behind health behaviours.
Morbidity is the level of illness in a population, measured by incidence (new cases in a given period) and prevalence (total existing cases at a point in time); mortality is the death rate.
Life expectancy is the average number of years a person is expected to live, based on current age- and sex-specific death rates.
Coronary heart disease remains the leading cause of death for Australian men; dementia (including Alzheimer's disease) is now the leading cause of death for Australian women.
Overweight and obesity overtook tobacco smoking as the leading contributor to Australia's overall disease burden in 2024.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples experience significantly poorer health status than non-Indigenous Australians, including a large gap in life expectancy and a higher prevalence of chronic disease — the Closing the Gap initiative targets this, connecting to both SDG 3 and SDG 10.

Other groups experiencing health inequities include people who are socioeconomically disadvantaged, people in rural and remote areas, culturally and linguistically diverse populations, people with disability, and older people.

Compared with other OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) countries, Australia's life expectancy (about 83 years) is roughly 1.9 years above the OECD average, and Australia ranks 10th highest of 38 OECD countries for health-adjusted life expectancy (HALE).

Australia has lower preventable and treatable mortality than the OECD average, and one of the lowest rates of death from cardiovascular disease among OECD countries — reflecting strong healthcare access and a lower daily smoking rate (8.5% versus an OECD average of 14.8%).

Cardiovascular disease and cancer are Australia's two largest contributors to burden of disease. Cancer's risk factors include smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, poor diet, UV exposure and family history, while its main protective factors are avoiding tobacco, limiting alcohol, sun protection and participating in national screening programs (e.g. for breast, cervical and bowel cancer) that support early detection.

Type 2 diabetes is a third major chronic condition alongside cardiovascular disease and cancer — its incidence and prevalence have been rising alongside overweight and obesity rates, and it disproportionately affects Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and older Australians. Risk factors include excess body weight, physical inactivity and family history; protective factors include maintaining a healthy weight, regular physical activity and a balanced diet, and early detection through regular check-ups.

People in rural and remote areas experience poorer health status than those in major cities — including lower life expectancy and higher rates of chronic disease and injury — largely due to reduced access to healthcare services and specialists, greater travel distances and cost, a smaller local health workforce, and higher rates of risk factors like smoking and hazardous alcohol use. Improving this requires expanding outreach and telehealth services, incentivising health professionals to work regionally, and targeted health promotion.

Healthy ageing is the process of developing and maintaining the functional ability that enables wellbeing in older age — remaining physically active, socially connected and engaged reduces reliance on health services and delays the need for residential aged care. A growing and ageing population is increasing demand on hospitals, aged care and chronic disease management, while placing growing strain on the volunteer organisations that support older Australians; government and non-government agencies need to plan for this by expanding aged care capacity, supporting healthy ageing programs, and adapting health services to a larger, older population.

groups.title: CQ2 — How does Australia's healthcare system work towards achieving better health for all Australians?
points: Australia has a mixed public/private healthcare system. Medicare, the universal public health insurance scheme, gives citizens and permanent residents access to free treatment in public hospitals and subsidised (or bulk-billed) visits to GPs and specialists.

Responsibility for the health system is shared across three levels of government: the federal government funds Medicare, national health policy and research; state and territory governments run public hospitals and community/mental health services; local government manages food hygiene, waste disposal, building standards and services like Meals on Wheels.

Private health insurance gives shorter waiting times for non-urgent treatment, choice of hospital and doctor, and cover for services (like dental and physiotherapy) that Medicare doesn't fully subsidise — at an ongoing cost to the individual.
The National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) and My Aged Care are Commonwealth-funded programs that sit alongside Medicare to support specific population groups.

Shared responsibility describes how government and non-government organisations (charities, community health services, private providers) collaborate to deliver person-centred care — care organised around an individual's needs and preferences rather than a single disease or service — for example a patient managing a chronic illness may see a publicly-funded GP, a privately-run specialist and a non-government support service, all coordinated around their circumstances.

Complementary and alternative healthcare approaches (e.g. naturopathy, acupuncture, health apps) have grown due to consumer interest in holistic and preventive care, multicultural acceptance of traditional practices, and increasing recognition — including rebates — from private health funds. They can be used as a preventive measure, to treat a health issue directly, or as a supplement alongside conventional medical treatment.
Being a critical health consumer means knowing how to assess the accuracy and credibility of health information, products and services before acting on them.

Ongoing challenges facing the healthcare system include the balance between healthcare spending and prevention, sustainability, equity of access (especially in rural and remote areas), privatisation, and hospital capacity.

groups.title: CQ3 — How is the growing and changing use of technology and data impacting Australia's healthcare system?
points: Technology affects health mainly through measuring (wearables like smartwatches and rings), monitoring (remote patient monitoring, e.g. glucometers for diabetes), early diagnosis (AI-assisted analysis of scans) and precision surgery and treatment (augmented reality, 3D-printed prosthetics and implants).

Digital health refers to the use of information and communication technology to manage health and wellbeing — including telehealth (remote consultations with healthcare providers), health apps, wearable devices and electronic health records. It aims to improve access (especially in rural and remote areas), reduce costs and connect health information across providers, though its success depends on internet access, digital literacy, and consistent uptake by both patients and healthcare providers.

My Health Record is Australia's national digital health record system — patients and their healthcare providers can securely access key health information, such as medications and test results, via myGov, the 1800MEDICARE app or the Healthdirect app.

The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) acts as the data custodian for My Health Record information used for research and public health purposes, and is responsible for its security and quality before release.

Big data in healthcare refers to the very large, complex datasets — hospital records, Medicare claims, wearable data — that are analysed to reduce healthcare spending, improve disease management, and inform policy, while raising challenges around the privacy and confidentiality of personal health information.

New technologies bring opportunities (less invasive procedures, faster recovery, earlier detection, greater precision) but also challenges (high cost, unequal access — especially in rural and remote areas — long wait times, and concerns about job impacts for health professionals).

groups.title: CQ4 — What actions are needed to promote and improve the health of Australians?
points: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are 17 global goals set by the United Nations in 2015, to be achieved by 2030, addressing poverty, inequality, health, education and environmental sustainability through the '5P' principles: People, Prosperity, Planet, Peace and Partnership.
SDG 3 (Good Health and Wellbeing) aims to ensure healthy lives and promote wellbeing for all ages, including reducing deaths from non-communicable diseases and ensuring universal health coverage.
SDG 4 (Quality Education) aims to ensure inclusive, equitable education and lifelong learning — health literacy education is closely linked to better health outcomes under SDG 3.
SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) aims to reduce inequality within and between countries, including income, access to resources, and social and political inclusion.
SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) aims to make cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable, including access to safe housing, green space and basic services.

The SDGs are interconnected: the NSW Healthy School Canteen Strategy links SDG 4 (health literacy education) with SDG 3 (better health outcomes); the Closing the Gap initiative links SDG 3 (health disparities) with SDG 10 (broader inequalities).

Healthy Cities Illawarra is a real example of the SDGs applied to a specific community — programs like Active In-Betweens, Cook Chill Chat and Food Fairness Illawarra apply SDG 3, 4 and 10 through physical activity, food education and equitable access to healthy food for the Illawarra region of NSW.

questions.questionHtml: Compare the health status of males and females in Australia.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Name the leading causes of mortality for each sex and note the difference.
  • Compare a measure of morbidity for each sex.
  • Compare life expectancy for each sex, with the current gap.
Sample answer

The top two leading causes of mortality (death rate) in males and females are coronary heart disease and dementia. However, the leading cause of death for women is dementia including Alzheimer's disease, whereas the leading cause of death for men is coronary heart disease. With regards to morbidity (rate of non-fatal sickness or disease), men are suffering mostly from coronary heart disease, back pain and problems and suicide. Women suffer from dementia, anxiety disorders and, thirdly, similar to males, back pain and problems. Although life expectancy for both genders is increasing, women are currently living longer than men (85 years for women and 81 years for men).

questions.questionHtml: Explain the role of epidemiology and how this information is useful.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • What epidemiology measures (life expectancy, causes of death, burden of disease).
  • Who uses this data and why — give at least one concrete example.
Sample answer

Epidemiology can provide health information about life expectancy, leading causes of death and burden of disease, as well as data about population groups who suffer poor health. This data can be used by government organisations to allocate funding, distribute resources to areas of greatest need and develop policies, as was seen during the Covid pandemic with public health orders such as lockdowns and mask mandates.

Both federal and state governments can be guided by this data to develop health promotion campaigns, e.g. 'Swap it, don't stop it' to raise awareness about ways to prevent chronic diseases causing a burden to Australia's health, e.g. heart disease and diabetes. Data about causes of hospitalisation and burden of disease can guide health departments and hospitals to recruit and train staff in areas of greatest need, e.g. more dementia care.

Epidemiology can also provide information about causes of disease which pharmaceutical companies can use to develop and market new products. In addition, data about the use of preventative measures such as immunisation, and information about risk behaviours such as alcohol consumption and drug use, can help doctors inform their patients about ways to improve their health.

questions.questionHtml: Compare Australia's life expectancy and health-adjusted life expectancy (HALE) with the OECD average.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • State Australia's life expectancy and how it compares to the OECD average.
  • State Australia's HALE ranking among OECD countries.
  • Link this to a possible explanation (healthcare access, smoking rates).
Sample answer

Australia's life expectancy is approximately 83 years, around 1.9 years above the OECD average. For health-adjusted life expectancy (HALE) — which estimates the years lived in full health, not just years alive — Australia ranks 10th highest of the 38 OECD countries, with Japan reporting the highest HALE and Mexico the lowest.

Australia's comparatively strong result is linked to lower rates of preventable and treatable mortality than the OECD average, one of the lowest rates of death from cardiovascular disease among OECD countries, and a daily smoking rate (8.5%) well below the OECD average of 14.8% — reflecting the impact of Australia's healthcare access and public health campaigns.

questions.questionHtml: Outline TWO groups most at risk of cancer in Australia.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Name two at-risk groups and the cancer type most relevant to each.
  • Give the risk factor connecting the group to that cancer.
Sample answer

Cancer involves a group of cells that abnormally develop. Malignant cancer cells can impact the body in a negative way and spread around major organs; other cells can be dominant and not cause harm (benign). Older women (over 40 years of age) are one group most at risk of developing breast cancer, in particular those who have children at a later stage of life. People who smoke are also most at risk of developing lung cancer, due to the harmful carcinogenic chemicals in tobacco harming the lungs, which are the primary gas exchange points in the body.

questions.questionHtml: Examine the impact of a growing and ageing population on the health system and services.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define a growing and ageing population and why it's occurring.
  • Link it to increased demand on hospitals, GPs and aged care.
  • Note the strain on volunteer/community-based care.
Sample answer

A growing and ageing population is the result of increased life expectancy and decreased birth rates. An ageing population impacts Australia's health system and services to a large extent. People aged 65 and over experience higher rates of hospital admissions and use GP services more frequently, accounting for around 1 in 4 emergency presentations, 42% of overnight hospital stays and 3 in 10 GP consultations (AIHW).

Over the last 20 years the proportion of people aged over 65 has increased from around 12% to 15%. This can place significant strain on hospital services and decrease the availability of GPs for the wider population. Additionally, people aged over 65 experience higher levels of chronic disease, with coronary heart disease and dementia being leading contributors to disability, which can cause a loss of independence and an inability to meet basic needs. As a result, an ageing population increases demand for aged care facilities, with the aged care sector needing to expand to meet this demand.

Volunteer organisations are also under strain, as these members of the community are ageing themselves and can only spend limited time assisting the aged. A healthy ageing population that engages in protective behaviours — remaining physically active, eating a balanced diet and maintaining social and community connections — can reduce these impacts by reducing the need for health services and delaying the need for residential aged care.

questions.questionHtml: Analyse the determinants of health that contribute to health inequities experienced by people in rural and remote Australia.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Name the group and state their overall health status compared with major cities.
  • Explain at least three determinants and how they interact.
  • Note an action that could address the inequity.
Sample answer

People in rural and remote areas experience poorer health status than those in major cities, including lower life expectancy and higher rates of chronic disease, injury and preventable hospitalisation. This is the result of several interacting determinants of health rather than any single cause.

Geographically, rural and remote communities are further from hospitals and specialists, meaning longer travel times and delayed treatment, especially for emergencies. Socioeconomically, these areas often have lower average incomes and fewer employment opportunities, making the added cost and time of travelling for care a greater burden. This is compounded by a biomedical factor: a smaller local health workforce, since many specialists and even GPs are concentrated in cities, leaving rural areas reliant on visiting services or telehealth. Environmental and social factors also interact here — rural communities report higher rates of risk behaviours such as smoking and hazardous alcohol use, partly linked to social isolation and fewer health promotion services reaching these areas.

Because these determinants compound one another — distance increases cost, cost reduces access, and reduced access allows risk behaviours and untreated conditions to persist — addressing the inequity requires more than one intervention, such as expanding telehealth and outreach clinics alongside incentives for health professionals to work regionally.

questions.questionHtml: Outline the health inequities faced by males in Australia.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Name the main mortality and morbidity gaps between males and females.
  • Link at least one gap to a behavioural or social cause.
Sample answer

Males in Australia have a lower life expectancy than females (around four years less) and higher rates of premature death from coronary heart disease, suicide and accidents. These gaps are linked to males engaging in more risky health behaviours, such as higher rates of risky alcohol consumption and lower rates of help-seeking for mental health issues, and to males being less likely to access preventative healthcare such as regular GP check-ups.

questions.questionHtml: Explain both the risk and protective factors of cancer.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Give risk factors across biological, behavioural and environmental categories.
  • Give protective factors and link them back to reducing specific risks.
  • Note that risk is cumulative — multiple factors interact.
Sample answer

Risk factors for cancer include biological factors such as family history and age, behavioural factors such as smoking, poor diet, physical inactivity and excessive alcohol consumption, and environmental factors such as UV exposure and exposure to carcinogens in some workplaces. These factors can act cumulatively, so a person with several risk factors has a substantially higher chance of developing cancer than someone with just one.

Protective factors work by reducing exposure to these risks: not smoking, maintaining a healthy weight and diet, staying physically active, limiting alcohol intake, using sun protection and participating in national screening programs (such as breast, bowel and cervical screening) so cancers are caught and treated early, when outcomes are far better.

questions.questionHtml: Australia's life expectancy at birth is ranked equal fourth among OECD countries. Explain reasons for why Australia's health ranking is high among OECD countries.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Link the ranking to Australia's healthcare system.
  • Link the ranking to lifestyle/behavioural factors.
  • Mention at least one specific example (Medicare, tobacco control).
Sample answer

Australia's high OECD health ranking is largely explained by its universal healthcare system, Medicare, which gives all citizens access to free or low-cost hospital and medical care regardless of income, meaning conditions are less likely to go untreated. Strong public health regulation has also played a role — Australia has some of the strictest tobacco control laws in the world (plain packaging, high excise, advertising bans), which has driven smoking rates down and reduced smoking-related mortality.

Comparatively high living standards, a well-funded public health system, and effective immunisation and screening programs (such as the National Immunisation Program and cancer screening) also contribute, catching and preventing disease before it becomes life-threatening.

questions.questionHtml: Examine the opportunities and challenges for an ageing population in Australia.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Give at least two opportunities (e.g. volunteering, mentorship, workforce experience).
  • Give at least two challenges (e.g. healthcare costs, workforce/aged care shortages, dependency ratio).
  • Weigh the two sides rather than just listing them.
Sample answer

An ageing population creates opportunities as older Australians are a large and growing source of unpaid volunteer work, informal childcare and mentorship, and many remain in the paid workforce longer, contributing valuable experience and skills. Increased longevity also reflects, and can reinforce, improvements in healthcare and living standards more broadly.

However, an ageing population also creates significant challenges. Healthcare expenditure rises as older Australians generally require more chronic disease management, hospital admissions and aged care services, straining the health budget. There is a shrinking proportion of working-age people relative to retirees (a rising dependency ratio), which increases pressure on the tax base, superannuation and pension systems, and there are workforce shortages in aged care and disability support that make it harder to meet growing demand for services.

On balance, the opportunities depend on older Australians remaining healthy and engaged for longer, while the challenges depend on how well the health and aged care systems are resourced to keep pace with demand.

questions.questionHtml: What are the responsibilities of each of the three levels of government for the delivery of health services in Australia?
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Name all three levels of government.
  • Give a distinct responsibility/example for each.
Sample answer

The three levels of government in Australia are the Federal, State and Local. They all have a pivotal role in the delivery of health services. The Federal Government is responsible for the formation of national health policies and the funding of health care. Their funds go towards residential care, Medicare services, health research, and public hospitals. The main responsibility of the State Government is to provide health and community services. Their principal functions include mental health services, home and community care and rehabilitation programs. The Local Government is responsible for environmental control such as waste disposal, food hygiene standards and monitoring building standards. They are also in charge of providing a range of preventative home care services such as Meals on Wheels.

questions.questionHtml: What are the benefits of Medicare for Australian citizens?
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • State who Medicare covers and at what cost.
  • Give at least two concrete benefits.
Sample answer

Medicare gives all Australian citizens access to basic healthcare facilities and services at minimal or no cost. It is advantageous for citizens as it provides access to treatment in public hospitals for procedures including heart surgery, access to specialists, and emergency health care. Medicare also provides access to a general practitioner at no cost through the bulk billing scheme.

questions.questionHtml: Outline advantages of an individual obtaining private health insurance cover.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Give at least three distinct advantages, with an example each.
Sample answer

Private health insurance has many advantages including shorter waiting times for elective and non-urgent treatments and being able to stay in a hospital of one's own choice in a private room. You are also able to have a doctor of your choice in hospital, and ancillary benefits such as dental cover and physiotherapy are subsidised. It provides the individual with security, protection and peace of mind.

questions.questionHtml: Outline the reasons for the growth of complementary and alternative health products and services.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Give several distinct reasons for the growth.
  • Support with a concrete example (e.g. a named service or provider behaviour).
Sample answer

There are many reasons for the growth of complementary and alternative health care products and services. A key reason is the endorsement by the World Health Organisation of the usefulness of many alternative approaches and of medicinal plants to be used in the preparation of herbal medicines. Many people are preferring to use natural or herbal medicines rather than synthetically produced medicines as part of their treatment, and enjoy a personal connection with their therapist. Many individuals are also attracted to the holistic nature of alternative products and services.

With Australia's multicultural heritage, there is increased acceptance and recognition of complementary and alternative health products and services such as shiatsu and acupuncture, which are traditional cultural practices particularly in Asian countries. There is also increased acceptance and recognition by GPs and specialists that alternative medicines can complement existing and prescribed traditional Western treatments. Many major private health funds now include complementary and alternative health services, e.g. chiropractic care and acupuncture, in their ancillary options and provide rebates.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the concept of shared responsibility in the Australian healthcare system, using an example.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define shared responsibility between government and non-government sectors.
  • Link it to person-centred care.
  • Give a concrete example.
Sample answer

Shared responsibility describes how government and non-government organisations collaborate, rather than working in isolation, to meet a person's health needs. Government provides the funding backbone through Medicare and public hospitals, while non-government organisations — including charities, community health services and private providers — deliver complementary services that government alone doesn't cover.

This collaboration supports person-centred care, where services are organised around an individual's full circumstances rather than a single disease. For example, a person managing a chronic illness like diabetes might see a bulk-billed GP (government-funded) for ongoing management, a private specialist for complications, and a non-government community health service for dietary and lifestyle support — with these providers ideally coordinating so the person isn't left to navigate the system alone. This shared approach improves continuity of care and can reduce the risk of a person falling through gaps between services.

questions.questionHtml: Identify three types of Primary healthcare and provide an example of how one of them is used in Australia.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • List three types (e.g. GP services, community health centres, allied health).
  • Give one concrete Australian example.
Sample answer

Three types of primary healthcare are general practitioner (GP) services, community health centres, and allied health services such as physiotherapy and dietetics. For example, GP services in Australia are accessed through Medicare, allowing patients to see a doctor for check-ups, referrals and management of ongoing conditions, often at no out-of-pocket cost through bulk billing.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how person-centred care differs from a more conventional, disease-focused approach to healthcare.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define person-centred care and disease-focused care.
  • Contrast at least two features (whose needs are prioritised, how decisions are made).
Sample answer

A conventional, disease-focused approach centres treatment around the illness itself, with the healthcare provider directing diagnosis and treatment with limited input from the patient. Person-centred care, by contrast, places the individual's needs, values and preferences at the centre of decision-making, involving the patient (and often their family) as active partners in planning their own care.

This means person-centred care considers a patient's social, emotional and cultural circumstances alongside their medical condition, rather than treating the disease in isolation, which can lead to better engagement with treatment and improved overall wellbeing.

questions.questionHtml: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of having private health insurance for the individual.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Give at least two advantages (choice of doctor/hospital, shorter waiting times, extras cover).
  • Give at least two disadvantages (ongoing premiums, out-of-pocket gaps, means-tested rebate/surcharge).
Sample answer

Private health insurance offers individuals advantages such as choice of doctor and hospital, generally shorter waiting times for elective surgery, and access to 'extras' cover for services Medicare doesn't fully fund, such as dental, physiotherapy and optical care.

However, it also has disadvantages: ongoing premiums can be expensive and tend to rise each year, policies often still involve out-of-pocket 'gap' payments, and higher-income earners who don't hold private hospital cover may pay the Medicare Levy Surcharge, adding a financial cost either way.

questions.questionHtml: Discuss the potential impact of privatisation on equity of access to healthcare in Australia. Your answer should consider both the potential advantages and disadvantages.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define what privatisation means in a healthcare context.
  • Discuss a potential advantage (efficiency, reduced public system pressure).
  • Discuss a potential disadvantage (cost as a barrier, widening inequity).
Sample answer

Privatisation involves shifting the delivery or funding of healthcare services from the public sector towards private providers. This can improve efficiency and reduce pressure on the public system, as patients with private cover use private hospitals rather than adding to public hospital waiting lists, freeing up public resources for those who cannot afford private care.

However, privatisation can also worsen equity of access, because private healthcare is only affordable to those who can pay premiums or out-of-pocket costs. This risks creating a two-tiered system where wealthier Australians access faster, higher-choice care while lower-income Australians rely solely on an increasingly stretched public system, widening health inequities between socioeconomic groups.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how My Health Record and big data are intended to improve Australia's healthcare system.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain what My Health Record is and how people access it.
  • Explain what big data is and how it's used.
  • Name who is responsible for the security/quality of this data.
Sample answer

My Health Record is Australia's national digital health record system. It lets patients and their healthcare providers securely access key health information, such as medications, allergies and test results, through myGov, the 1800MEDICARE app or the Healthdirect app — reducing the risk of information being lost or duplicated between different providers.

Big data refers to the very large, complex datasets generated across the healthcare system, including hospital records, Medicare claims and My Health Record data. Analysing this data can identify patterns in disease and treatment outcomes, helping to reduce healthcare spending, improve disease management and inform government policy. The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) acts as the data custodian for My Health Record information used for research and public health purposes, and is responsible for ensuring its security and quality — which is important given the sensitivity of personal health information and the need to protect individuals' privacy.

questions.questionHtml: Evaluate the extent to which digital health has been successful in connecting Australia's health information.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define digital health and give examples of services.
  • Evaluate successes.
  • Evaluate limitations/challenges.
Sample answer

Digital health refers to the use of information and communication technology to manage health and wellbeing, including telehealth consultations, health apps, wearable devices and My Health Record. It has succeeded in connecting health information to a significant extent — My Health Record allows a patient's medications, allergies and test results to be viewed by any treating provider with the patient's consent, reducing duplicated tests and improving continuity of care, particularly for patients who see multiple specialists.

Telehealth has also been successful in connecting rural and remote patients to specialists who would otherwise require significant travel, improving equity of access. However, success has been uneven: uptake of My Health Record by both patients and healthcare providers has been inconsistent, meaning records are sometimes incomplete, and digital health relies on reliable internet access and digital literacy, which disadvantages older Australians, some rural communities, and people experiencing socioeconomic disadvantage. Privacy and data security concerns can also make some patients reluctant to engage fully with digital health services.

Overall, digital health has meaningfully improved the connection of health information for many Australians, but its benefits are not yet equally distributed, and closing these gaps in access and engagement remains an ongoing challenge for the healthcare system.

questions.questionHtml: Identify three examples of Artificial Intelligence being used in healthcare.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • List three distinct AI applications.
Sample answer

Examples of AI in Australian healthcare include AI-assisted analysis of medical imaging (such as detecting abnormalities in X-rays and scans), AI-driven diagnostic decision-support tools that help clinicians identify likely conditions from symptoms and test results, and AI-powered chatbots or virtual health assistants that provide basic triage and health information to patients.

questions.questionHtml: Outline the intended purposes of My Health Record and its role in the Australian healthcare system.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • State what My Health Record is.
  • Give at least two intended purposes (continuity of care, reduced duplication).
Sample answer

My Health Record is a secure, national digital summary of an individual's key health information, accessible by the patient and their treating healthcare providers. It is intended to improve continuity of care by letting different providers — GPs, specialists, hospitals and pharmacists — see a patient's history, medications and test results in one place, reducing duplicated tests, medication errors and gaps in communication between providers.

questions.questionHtml: Describe the role of wearable sensors in monitoring health data.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Describe what wearable sensors track.
  • Link this to a benefit for the individual or provider.
Sample answer

Wearable sensors, such as smartwatches and fitness trackers, continuously monitor health data including heart rate, sleep patterns, physical activity and, in some devices, blood oxygen levels or ECG readings. This allows individuals to track their own health trends over time and can alert users or healthcare providers to irregularities, supporting earlier detection of issues and more informed, real-time management of chronic conditions.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how telehealth services can improve access to healthcare. Provide examples.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain the barrier telehealth addresses (distance, mobility, time).
  • Give at least one concrete example.
  • Note a limitation to keep the answer balanced.
Sample answer

Telehealth services allow patients to consult healthcare providers remotely via phone or video call, which improves access to healthcare for people who face barriers to attending in person — such as those in rural and remote areas far from specialists, people with mobility issues, or those who cannot easily take time off work. For example, a patient in regional NSW can consult a city-based specialist via video call rather than travelling hours for an appointment, and GPs can conduct routine follow-up consultations by phone.

This reduces travel time and cost and can shorten waiting times for specialist advice, though telehealth is less suitable for conditions requiring physical examination or urgent, hands-on treatment.

groups.title: Actions to improve health — the SDGs

questions.questionHtml: Explain how the Sustainable Development Goals have been applied to improve health outcomes in a specific Australian community.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Name the community and the relevant SDGs.
  • Describe at least two concrete programs and which SDG(s) they address.
  • Explain the intended impact.
Sample answer

Healthy Cities Illawarra is a real example of the SDGs being applied to improve health in a specific community — the Illawarra region of New South Wales. Under SDG 3 (Good Health and Wellbeing), the 'Active In-Betweens' program promotes physical activity, nutrition and positive social experiences for 9–12-year-olds in vulnerable communities, while 'Play Illawarra' encourages families to use local parks and playgrounds to support physical activity and community connection.

The 'Cook Chill Chat' program addresses both SDG 3 and SDG 4 (Quality Education), building healthy eating habits and food-planning life skills while supporting mental wellbeing and social connection in a supportive setting. 'Food Fairness Illawarra' addresses SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) by working to ensure fair access to affordable, healthy food, particularly for low-income and vulnerable populations.

Together, these programs show how tailoring the SDGs to a community's specific needs — rather than treating each goal in isolation — can improve health literacy, food security and social connection, all of which contribute to better overall health status for that community.

questions.questionHtml: Outline the key features of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 10: Reduced Inequalities.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • State the overall aim of SDG 10.
  • Give one or two specific features/targets.
Sample answer

SDG 10 aims to reduce inequality within and among countries, including inequalities based on income, age, sex, disability, race and other status. Its key features include promoting social, economic and political inclusion for all, ensuring equal opportunity, and reducing inequalities of outcome, for example by adopting policies that support lower-income and marginalised groups.

questions.questionHtml: Describe the role of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 11: Sustainable Cities and Communities in improving health status for all Australians.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • State what SDG 11 targets.
  • Link at least one feature of sustainable cities directly to a health outcome.
Sample answer

SDG 11 aims to make cities and communities inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable, which supports health through improved access to safe and affordable housing, green public spaces, reliable public transport and clean air. For example, communities with well-designed green spaces and walkable infrastructure encourage physical activity, while affordable and safe housing reduces stress and exposure to health hazards, together improving both physical and mental health status across the population.

questions.questionHtml: Describe the relationship between Sustainable Development Goal 3 and Sustainable Development Goal 10 in improving health outcomes.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • State what SDG 3 and SDG 10 each target.
  • Explain how progress on one supports progress on the other.
Sample answer

SDG 3 (Good Health and Wellbeing) aims to ensure healthy lives and promote wellbeing for all, while SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) aims to reduce inequality within and between populations. The two goals are closely linked because health inequities are often driven by broader social and economic inequalities — for example, low-income groups typically have poorer access to healthcare, housing and nutrition. Progress on SDG 10, such as improving income equality and access to services for disadvantaged groups, therefore directly supports progress on SDG 3, as reducing inequality removes barriers that prevent disadvantaged groups from achieving good health outcomes.

questions.questionHtml: Justify the application of Sustainable Development Goals 3 and 4 to reduce mortality rates from cardiovascular disease.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain what SDG 3 and SDG 4 each target.
  • Justify how SDG 3 initiatives (health promotion, screening) reduce CVD mortality.
  • Justify how SDG 4 (education) contributes indirectly, and conclude with an overall judgement.
Sample answer

SDG 3 (Good Health and Wellbeing) directly supports reducing cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality through initiatives such as national health promotion campaigns targeting smoking, diet and physical inactivity, and through funding for screening programs and improved access to primary healthcare that allow early detection of risk factors such as high blood pressure and high cholesterol. These interventions are well justified because CVD is largely preventable, and early, low-cost interventions (such as GP screening) prevent far more costly and severe outcomes later.

SDG 4 (Quality Education) contributes indirectly but significantly, as health literacy gained through education helps individuals understand risk factors and make informed lifestyle choices, such as improving diet and increasing physical activity, while education also improves employment prospects and income, which in turn improves access to healthcare and healthier living conditions.

Applying both SDGs together is justified because they address CVD from complementary angles — SDG 3 through direct clinical and preventative health measures, and SDG 4 through the underlying social determinants that shape health behaviour — meaning the combined approach is more effective than either goal applied in isolation.

trivia.questionHtml: What is epidemiology?
trivia.answerHtml: The branch of medical science that studies the causes, distribution and control of disease and injury in populations.

trivia.questionHtml: What's the difference between incidence and prevalence?
trivia.answerHtml: Incidence is the number of new cases in a given period; prevalence is the total number of existing cases at a given time.

trivia.questionHtml: Which condition is currently Australia's leading cause of death for women?
trivia.answerHtml: Dementia, including Alzheimer's disease.

trivia.questionHtml: Which condition remains the leading cause of death for Australian men?
trivia.answerHtml: Coronary heart disease (CHD).

trivia.questionHtml: What is atherosclerosis?
trivia.answerHtml: The build-up of fatty and/or fibrous material on the interior walls of arteries.

trivia.questionHtml: What is arteriosclerosis?
trivia.answerHtml: A disease causing a general loss of elasticity ("hardening") of the arteries.

trivia.questionHtml: Which risk factor overtook tobacco smoking as Australia's leading contributor to disease burden in 2024?
trivia.answerHtml: Overweight and obesity.

trivia.questionHtml: What does OECD stand for?
trivia.answerHtml: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

trivia.questionHtml: How does Australia's life expectancy compare with the OECD average?
trivia.answerHtml: About 83 years — roughly 1.9 years above the OECD average.

trivia.questionHtml: Where does Australia rank for health-adjusted life expectancy (HALE) among OECD countries?
trivia.answerHtml: 10th highest of 38 OECD countries.

trivia.questionHtml: What is Medicare?
trivia.answerHtml: Australia's universal public health insurance scheme, giving citizens and permanent residents access to free or subsidised healthcare.

trivia.questionHtml: Which level of government mainly funds and operates public hospitals in Australia?
trivia.answerHtml: State and territory governments.

trivia.questionHtml: Which level of government is responsible for food hygiene standards, waste disposal and building standards?
trivia.answerHtml: Local government.

trivia.questionHtml: What does NDIS stand for?
trivia.answerHtml: National Disability Insurance Scheme.

trivia.questionHtml: What is My Health Record?
trivia.answerHtml: Australia's national digital health record system, letting patients and their healthcare providers securely access key health information online.

trivia.questionHtml: Who is the data custodian of My Health Record information used for research and public health purposes?
trivia.answerHtml: The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW).

trivia.questionHtml: What does "big data" in healthcare refer to?
trivia.answerHtml: Very large, complex datasets — e.g. hospital records, Medicare claims, wearable data — analysed to find patterns that improve health outcomes.

trivia.questionHtml: How many Sustainable Development Goals did the UN set in 2015?
trivia.answerHtml: 17 goals, to be achieved by 2030.

trivia.questionHtml: Which SDG specifically targets "Good Health and Wellbeing"?
trivia.answerHtml: SDG 3.

trivia.questionHtml: Name the four SDGs specifically studied in this course.
trivia.answerHtml: SDG 3 (Good Health and Wellbeing), SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities).

trivia.questionHtml: What real-world initiative applies the SDGs to health in the Illawarra region of NSW?
trivia.answerHtml: Healthy Cities Illawarra.

trivia.questionHtml: What national initiative addresses the health and life-expectancy gap for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples?
trivia.answerHtml: Closing the Gap.

trivia.questionHtml: Besides cardiovascular disease and cancer, what is a third major chronic condition examined in this course?
trivia.answerHtml: Type 2 diabetes.

trivia.questionHtml: Name two reasons people in rural and remote areas have poorer health status than those in major cities.
trivia.answerHtml: Reduced access to healthcare services/specialists and a smaller local health workforce (also: distance, cost, higher rates of risk behaviours).

trivia.questionHtml: What is healthy ageing?
trivia.answerHtml: The process of developing and maintaining the functional ability that enables wellbeing in older age.

trivia.questionHtml: What is shared responsibility in the Australian healthcare system?
trivia.answerHtml: Government and non-government organisations collaborating to deliver person-centred care.

trivia.questionHtml: What is person-centred care?
trivia.answerHtml: Care organised around an individual's needs and preferences, rather than a single disease or service.

trivia.questionHtml: What is digital health?
trivia.answerHtml: The use of information and communication technology to manage health and wellbeing — e.g. telehealth, health apps, wearables and My Health Record.
